Eta Squared (Effect Size for ANOVA)

Source: R/eta_squared.R
eta_squared.Rd

Computes the sample eta squared (\(\eta^2\)) of each effect of an analysis of variance, the proportion of the variance of the dependent variable that the effect accounts for, as two estimands: the total \(\eta^2\), the effect's sum of squares as a proportion of the corrected total sum of squares, and the partial \(\eta^2\), its sum of squares as a proportion of its own sum of squares and the error sum of squares. With estimand = "all", the default, the function reports every estimand its inputs determine; "total" or "partial" reports one. In a one-way design the two are the same number.

Usage

eta_squared(
  object = NULL,
  estimand = c("all", "total", "partial"),
  SS_effect = NULL,
  SS_error = NULL,
  SS_total = NULL,
  F_value = NULL,
  df_effect = NULL,
  df_error = NULL
)

Arguments

object

Optional. A fitted model of class aov, lm, or aovlist (a multi-stratum fit such as aov(y ~ A + Error(subject/A), data = d)). The function returns one row per effect (every row of anova(object), or of each stratum of summary(object), other than Residuals), with the stratum named for an aovlist. Give either object or summary statistics, not both.

estimand

Which estimand to report: "all" (the default, every estimand the inputs determine, NA for the others), "total", or "partial". An estimand asked for by name that the inputs do not determine is refused (see Details).

SS_effect

The sum of squares of the effect, or a vector of the sums of squares of several effects of one analysis (named for the effects, which label the rows).

SS_error

The error (residual) sum of squares. With SS_effect, it determines the partial \(\eta^2\).

SS_total

The corrected total sum of squares, \(\sum (y - \bar{y})^2\) (see Details). With SS_effect, it determines the total \(\eta^2\).

F_value

The observed F statistic of the effect, or a vector of the F statistics of several effects tested against the same error term. With df_effect and df_error, it determines the partial \(\eta^2\) only.

df_effect

The numerator degrees of freedom of the effect (one value for each effect, or one for all). Required with F_value; with sums of squares it is optional and, with df_error and SS_error, fills the F_value column.

df_error

The error (residual) degrees of freedom. Required with F_value; optional with sums of squares.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_anova_es, printed through dmar_tbl) with one row per effect and the columns effect, eta_squared_total and eta_squared_partial (only the one asked for when estimand is "total" or "partial"), stratum (for an aovlist fit), F_value, df_effect, and df_error. An effect given through the summary interfaces without names is "overall" (or effect_1, effect_2, and so on, for several), and a quantity the inputs do not give (the F statistic of sums of squares given without degrees of freedom) is NA. The estimand attribute records the estimand asked for, and the estimand_notes attribute names each estimand column that is NA with the reason, which the line beneath the printed table states. tidy() gives one row per effect and estimand (see dmar_tidiers).

Details

The function takes a fitted model (aov, lm, or an aovlist from aov() with an Error() term), the sums of squares of a published ANOVA table, or an F statistic with its degrees of freedom. The confidence interval is computed by ci_eta_squared.

Total and partial. For an effect with sum of squares \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}}\), error sum of squares \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{error}}\), and corrected total sum of squares \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{total}}\), $$\hat{\eta}^2_{\text{total}} = \frac{\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}}}{\mathit{SS}_{\text{total}}}, \qquad \hat{\eta}^2_{\text{partial}} = \frac{\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}}}{\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}} + \mathit{SS}_{\text{error}}} = \frac{df_{\text{effect}} F}{df_{\text{effect}} F + df_{\text{error}}}$$ (Olejnik & Algina, 2000, Table 10, p. 268; Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Eqs. 7.40 to 7.42). The total value is a proportion of all the variation in the data, and so depends on the other factors of the design: adding a factor with a large effect lowers it. The partial value leaves the other effects out of its denominator, so the partial values of the effects of one design do not share a denominator and can sum to more than 1 (Olejnik & Algina, 2000, pp. 268–269). Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Chapter 7) frame the choice by the other factors: when another factor is extrinsic to the question (a study of the effect could as well hold it constant, as a study of drugs could hold biofeedback constant) the partial value answers it, and when the factor is intrinsic (it varies wherever the effect is studied, as gender does) the total value does. In a one-way design \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{total}} = \mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}} + \mathit{SS}_{\text{error}}\), and the two estimands are the same number.

What the inputs determine. A fitted model determines both estimands of every effect, and so do sums of squares that include both SS_error and SS_total. SS_effect with SS_total alone determines the total, and with SS_error alone the partial. An F statistic and its degrees of freedom determine the partial value only: the total of an effect also depends on the sums of squares of the design's other effects (from the F statistics of every effect it can be written as \(df_{\text{effect}} F / (\sum df F + df_{\text{error}})\), Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Eq. 7.43, which a fitted model provides). The function cannot tell from F whether the design has other effects, so the F interface reports the total as NA even for a one-way design, where it equals the partial value. With estimand = "all" an estimand the inputs do not determine is NA, with the reason in the estimand_notes attribute and beneath the printed table; asked for by name, it is refused with an error of class dmar_estimand_undetermined (see dmar_metadata). Sums of squares and F are two ways of giving the same effect, and a call that gives both, or a fitted model with summary statistics, is refused, as is a set of sums of squares in which SS_effect + SS_error exceeds SS_total.

The corrected total. SS_total is the corrected total sum of squares, \(\sum (y - \bar{y})^2\), the sum of every sum of squares of an ANOVA table with an intercept, the error included. Some programs also print an uncorrected total, \(\sum y^2\), which includes the grand mean: Kim (2016, Table 3) lists both, a “Total” of 53758.357 and a “Corrected total” of 5863.715, and the second is SS_total. A fitted model without an intercept does not partition the corrected total, and its total \(\eta^2\) is NA.

Sums of squares of a fitted model. The sums of squares and F statistics of a fitted model are those of anova() (one stratum) or summary() (an aovlist), which are Type I (sequential): each effect is adjusted for the effects before it in the formula. Sequential sums of squares add up to the corrected total, so the total \(\eta^2\) of every effect and the error's share sum to 1. In a balanced design Types I, II, and III agree; in an unbalanced one they differ, and the order of the terms changes the Type I values. For Type II or III sums of squares, compute them with, for example, car::Anova(object, type = 3), and give the effect's sum of squares with the error and corrected total sums of squares to the sums-of-squares interface (Type III sums of squares need not add up to the total in an unbalanced design, so the total values of the effects then need not sum with the error's share to 1). Type III tests depend on how the factors are coded. The Type III main-effect tests compare unweighted marginal means only when the factors are coded with contrasts that sum to zero over their levels, such as contr.sum (contr.helmert and contr.poly also qualify). Under R's default treatment contrasts, the Type III test of a factor that enters an interaction compares its levels only at the reference levels of the factors it interacts with, which is seldom the hypothesis intended. Set the coding before the model is fitted, either in the call (lm(y ~ A * B, data = d, contrasts = list(A = contr.sum, B = contr.sum))) or for the session (options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))). The help page of car::Anova() gives the same warning, and notes that when a model has numeric covariates and interactions, the Type III test of a factor compares the groups where the covariates are 0; Type II tests do not depend on the coding. factorial_anova applies sum-to-zero contrasts itself and reports partial \(\eta^2\) and partial \(\omega^2\) with their confidence intervals for between-subjects factorial designs.

Interactions and covariates. An interaction is an effect like any other, with its own sum of squares and degrees of freedom, and so is a covariate of an lm fit: each is a row, its partial value computed against the error, its total against the corrected total.

Within-subjects designs. For an aovlist fit, each effect's partial \(\eta^2\) is computed against the error of its own stratum, so a within-subjects factor's partial value leaves the differences among subjects out of its denominator. Its total value divides by the corrected total over all strata (the sum of every sum of squares that summary(object) reports), which includes the differences among subjects: in a design with one within-subjects factor the total value is the factor's sum of squares over the sum of those for subjects, the factor, and their interaction (Bakeman, 2005, p. 380), and is smaller than the partial value. Neither is comparable with the same effect in a between-subjects design; see eta_squared_generalized for an index that is (Olejnik & Algina, 2003; Bakeman, 2005). Other model classes (lmerMod, lme) are not taken; give their sums of squares or F statistics to the summary interfaces.

References

Bakeman, R. (2005). Recommended effect size statistics for repeated measures designs. Behavior Research Methods, 37(3), 379–384. doi:10.3758/BF03192707

Bargmann, R. E. (1970). Interpretation and use of a generalized discriminant function. In R. C. Bose, I. M. Chakravarti, P. C. Mahalanobis, C. R. Rao, & K. J. C. Smith (Eds.), Essays in probability and statistics (pp. 35–60). University of North Carolina Press.

Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

Fleishman, A. I. (1980). Confidence intervals for correlation ratios. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 40(3), 659–670. doi:10.1177/001316448004000309

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Preacher, K. J. (2012). On effect size. Psychological Methods, 17, 137–152. doi:10.1037/a0028086

Kim, H.-Y. (2016). Statistical notes for clinical researchers: Sample size calculation 3. Comparison of several means using one-way ANOVA. Restorative Dentistry & Endodontics, 41(3), 231–234. doi:10.5395/rde.2016.41.3.231

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on \(\eta^2\), Chapter 7 on factorial designs, and Chapter 11 on generalized \(\eta^2\) for within-subjects designs.)

Olejnik, S., & Algina, J. (2000). Measures of effect size for comparative studies: Applications, interpretations, and limitations. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 25(3), 241–286. doi:10.1006/ceps.2000.1040

Olejnik, S., & Algina, J. (2003). Generalized eta and omega squared statistics: Measures of effect size for some common research designs. Psychological Methods, 8(4), 434–447. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.4.434

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the analysis of variance and contrast analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164

Venables, W. (1975). Calculation of confidence intervals for noncentrality parameters. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 37(3), 406–412. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1975.tb01554.x

Examples

# 1. The sums of squares of a published two-way table: Kim (2016,
#    Table 3), light by material, 2 by 4 with 10 per cell (N = 80).
#    SS_total is the corrected total, 5863.715.
eta_squared(SS_effect = c(LIGHT = 34.716, MATERIAL = 1996.998,
                          "LIGHT:MATERIAL" = 1570.389),
            SS_error = 2261.612, SS_total = 5863.715,
            df_effect = c(1, 3, 3), df_error = 72)
#>  effect         eta_squared_total eta_squared_partial F_value df_effect
#>  LIGHT          0.006             0.015               1.105   1        
#>  MATERIAL       0.341             0.469               21.192  3        
#>  LIGHT:MATERIAL 0.268             0.410               16.665  3        
#>  df_error
#>  72      
#>  72      
#>  72      

# 2. An F statistic and its degrees of freedom determine the partial
#    value only. Bargmann's (1970) example, used in turn by Venables
#    (1975), Fleishman (1980), and Steiger (2004): a one-way ANOVA with
#    five groups of 11 and an observed F of 11.221 on 4 and 50 df. In a
#    one-way design the partial value is the total.
eta_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50,
            estimand = "partial")
#>  effect  eta_squared_partial F_value df_effect df_error
#>  overall 0.473               11.221  4         50      

# 3. One-way ANOVA from a fitted model (depression_bdi: three
#    treatment arms, 10 per arm, N = 30); the two estimands agree.
fit_one <- aov(bdi_post ~ condition, data = depression_bdi)
eta_squared(fit_one)
#>  effect    eta_squared_total eta_squared_partial F_value df_effect df_error
#>  condition 0.184             0.184               3.035   2         27      

# 4. Factorial ANOVA (pygmalion: expectancy treatment by grade, 2 by 6
#    with unequal cell sizes, N = 310). The treatment is manipulated;
#    grade is a measured classification of the pupils.
fit_factorial <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment * factor(grade), data = pygmalion)
eta_squared(fit_factorial)
#>  effect                  eta_squared_total eta_squared_partial F_value
#>  treatment               0.020             0.021               6.539  
#>  factor(grade)           0.043             0.045               2.795  
#>  treatment:factor(grade) 0.018             0.020               1.191  
#>  df_effect df_error
#>  1         298     
#>  5         298     
#>  5         298     

# 5. Within-subjects ANOVA: 20 simulated subjects, each measured at Pre,
#    Mid, and Post. The total value includes the differences among
#    subjects in its denominator; the partial value does not.
set.seed(113)
n <- 20
rm_data <- data.frame(
  subject = factor(rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)),
  time    = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), n),
                   levels = c("Pre", "Mid", "Post")),
  y       = rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)[rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)] +
            0.7 * rep(1:3, n) + rnorm(n * 3, sd = 1.2)
)
fit_rm <- aov(y ~ time + Error(subject/time), data = rm_data)
eta_squared(fit_rm)
#>  effect eta_squared_total eta_squared_partial stratum      F_value df_effect
#>  time   0.097             0.231               subject:time 5.701   2        
#>  df_error
#>  38
